cards.scenario: Both options work. Stem says 'minimal changes' and 'no code changes'.
cards.ok: The option needing no application changes
cards.bad: The cleaner re-architecture with better long-term design
cards.why: The constraint word is what picks between two working options.

cards.scenario: Video transcoding at scale: Lambda/SQS/EC2 pipeline or a purpose-built AWS service?
cards.ok: AWS Elemental MediaConvert
cards.bad: Custom Lambda, SQS and EC2 transcoding pipeline
cards.why: Managed service beats DIY whenever one exists for the job.

cards.scenario: Nightly report, short deadline, 'quick' in the stem. Query data in S3.
cards.ok: Athena
cards.bad: Provision a Redshift cluster and load the data
cards.why: Don't overbuild: pick the lightest feature that works.

cards.scenario: Don't block developers; flag non-compliant resources and fix them automatically.
cards.ok: AWS Config rule with auto-remediation
cards.bad: SCP that denies the non-compliant action
cards.why: Detect is not prevent: SCP or IAM deny blocks, Config detects.

cards.scenario: Choose TWO. One pair contains an option with a self-contradicting clause.
cards.ok: The pair that completes one solution together
cards.bad: Two individually strong options from different solutions
cards.why: Both picks must finish the same solution; one wrong clause kills an option.

cards.scenario: Stem says 'serverless'. Pick compute and database.
cards.ok: Fargate with Aurora Serverless
cards.bad: ECS on EC2 with provisioned RDS
cards.why: Serverless in the stem rules out anything with servers to manage.

cards.scenario: Two options identical except 'Deep Archive' vs 'Infrequent Access'.
cards.ok: Judge only the differing phrase against the retrieval requirement
cards.bad: Pick the cheaper storage class without comparing further
cards.why: Twin options differ by one phrase; that phrase decides.

cards.scenario: Single-answer question. First pick fits; on review another option looks more complete, but no stem phrase rules out the first.
cards.ok: Keep the first pick
cards.bad: Switch to the option that feels more complete
cards.why: Review changes without new evidence broke right answers in Neal C and Udemy #2.

cards.scenario: Desktop app needs a 99.5% uptime SLA; minimize changes and costs. RDS is single-AZ today.
cards.ok: Keep single-AZ RDS; it already meets 99.5%
cards.bad: Upgrade RDS to Multi-AZ
cards.why: Match the SLA, don't exceed it at extra cost.

cards.scenario: Increase resilience across multiple AZs. App uses one NAT gateway and DynamoDB tables.
cards.ok: Deploy a NAT gateway in each AZ
cards.bad: Convert to DynamoDB global tables
cards.why: DynamoDB is already multi-AZ; the single NAT gateway is the zonal failure point.

cards.scenario: Projected EC2 cost may exceed budget. Notify the CFO; LOWEST risk of overspending.
cards.ok: Budgets forecast alert plus a Budgets action that stops instances
cards.bad: Budgets alert to an operator who stops instances manually
cards.why: Automation beats a human step; manual delay leaves overspend risk.

cards.scenario: Corporate IdP supports SAML; staff need AWS console access.
cards.ok: IAM Identity Center / AssumeRoleWithSAML
cards.bad: AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity
cards.why: SAML federation uses the SAML APIs, not web identity.

cards.scenario: Mobile app users sign in with social accounts and need AWS access.
cards.ok: Cognito with AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity temporary credentials
cards.bad: IAM users with access keys embedded in the app
cards.why: Social/mobile/SPA means web identity and temp creds, never keys.

cards.scenario: Third-party vendor assumes a role in your account; prevent confused deputy.
cards.ok: Trust policy requiring an sts:ExternalId condition
cards.bad: Share an IAM user's access keys with the vendor
cards.why: ExternalId is the third-party cross-account safeguard.

cards.scenario: GitHub Actions pipeline deploys to AWS without long-lived credentials.
cards.ok: IAM OIDC identity provider with an assumable role
cards.bad: IAM user access keys stored as repository secrets
cards.why: CI with OIDC gets short-lived credentials via STS.

cards.scenario: Cross-account role access fails. Fix it least-privilege.
cards.ok: Edit the target role's trust policy to name the caller's role ARN
cards.bad: Trust the caller account's root in the target role
cards.why: The role lives in the target account; a role ARN is tighter than the root.

cards.scenario: SCP allows a service but users in the OU still can't use it.
cards.ok: Also attach an IAM policy that grants the access
cards.bad: Add more Allow statements to the SCP
cards.why: An SCP never grants; it only filters what IAM can grant.

cards.scenario: A deny is needed for one OU only.
cards.ok: Attach the SCP deny at that OU
cards.bad: Attach the deny at the root
cards.why: A root deny hits every OU beneath it.

cards.scenario: Protect resources carrying a specific tag from deletion.
cards.ok: SCP deny with an aws:ResourceTag condition
cards.bad: Require MFA for all IAM users
cards.why: MFA is authentication, not authorization to a tagged resource.

cards.scenario: Enforce allowed tag values; developers must not be able to skip them.
cards.ok: Tag policy plus SCP denying creation without aws:RequestTag
cards.bad: AWS Config rule that flags untagged resources
cards.why: Enforce means prevent, so SCP; Config only detects.

cards.scenario: Restrict S3 access points to VPC-only use across the organization.
cards.ok: SCP with the s3:AccessPointNetworkOrigin condition
cards.bad: Bucket policy allowing a list of source IP ranges
cards.why: The condition key on access point creation enforces network origin.

cards.scenario: Only principals from our AWS Organization may use an ECR repo or S3 bucket.
cards.ok: Resource policy with aws:PrincipalOrgID
cards.bad: List every member account ID in the policy
cards.why: PrincipalOrgID scales and follows org membership automatically.

cards.scenario: Central backups with retention, cross-Region copy and failure alerts.
cards.ok: AWS Backup plan with a copy action and SNS
cards.bad: DLM snapshot policy plus custom Lambda copy glue
cards.why: AWS Backup is the managed, centralized answer.

cards.scenario: Company already runs Microsoft AD and wants SSO to AWS.
cards.ok: Directory Service Managed AD with trust, then SSO
cards.bad: Recreate every user in IAM Identity Center
cards.why: Reuse the existing directory instead of duplicating identities.

cards.scenario: DB credentials need automatic rotation and injection into ECS tasks.
cards.ok: Secrets Manager via ECS secrets/valueFrom
cards.bad: Systems Manager Parameter Store SecureString
cards.why: Rotation and lifecycle are Secrets Manager features.

cards.scenario: Deploy a stack to every org account, including future accounts.
cards.ok: StackSets with service-managed permissions and auto-deploy
cards.bad: Self-managed StackSets with per-account IAM roles
cards.why: Service-managed plus auto-deploy covers new accounts automatically.

cards.scenario: Allocate costs by tag across the organization.
cards.ok: Activate cost allocation tags in the management account plus CUR
cards.bad: Activate the tags separately in each member account
cards.why: Tags are activated in the management account.

cards.scenario: Developers need self-service launch of approved stacks, minimal IAM rights.
cards.ok: Service Catalog products with a launch constraint role
cards.bad: Grant developers CloudFormation and resource permissions directly
cards.why: The launch constraint role acts on their behalf.

cards.scenario: CloudTrail logs must be tamper-proof.
cards.ok: Log file validation plus MFA Delete on the bucket
cards.bad: SSE-KMS encryption on the log bucket
cards.why: KMS gives confidentiality only, not integrity.

cards.scenario: Notify and auto-fix when someone calls CreateUser.
cards.ok: CloudTrail to EventBridge rule, then Step Functions/Lambda and SNS
cards.bad: AWS Config periodic rule evaluating IAM users
cards.why: An API call is an event: EventBridge reacts in near real time.

cards.scenario: Organizations: CCoE must enforce daily EBS backups consistently across all accounts; MOST reliable.
cards.ok: Organizations backup policy driving AWS Backup plans
cards.bad: Backup policy using Data Lifecycle Manager
cards.why: Org backup policies are an AWS Backup feature; DLM is per-account lifecycle.

cards.scenario: Protect S3, EBS, EFS, RDS and Volume Gateway data across Regions; automate; LEAST overhead.
cards.ok: AWS Backup plan with cross-Region copy to a vault
cards.bad: AWS Backup plus RDS cross-Region read replicas
cards.why: Replicas aren't backups and add overhead; AWS Backup already covers RDS.

cards.scenario: Deploy Config rules to nearly all accounts incl. management, exclude a few; members must not modify them.
cards.ok: Organization conformance pack via a delegated admin
cards.bad: StackSets plus drift detection
cards.why: Drift detection only detects changes; it doesn't prevent them.

cards.scenario: WorkSpaces users sign in with on-prem AD credentials; credentials must not be stored outside the company.
cards.ok: AD Connector
cards.bad: AWS Managed Microsoft AD with a trust
cards.why: AD Connector is a proxy; Managed AD creates a directory in AWS.

cards.scenario: 500 workloads in separate accounts; security and infra teams; a few unique workloads. Account structure?
cards.ok: Separate Log Archive, Security Tooling and Audit accounts plus an Exceptions OU
cards.bad: One central security account for logging, tooling and audit
cards.why: Separating them limits blast radius.

cards.scenario: SQS queue shared across org accounts. Identify principals outside the org that can access it.
cards.ok: IAM Access Analyzer with the organization as zone of trust
cards.bad: CloudTrail data events
cards.why: Who CAN access = policy analysis; CloudTrail only shows who DID call.

cards.scenario: HR and Recruiting share SCP requirements; Recruiting needs stricter ones. Avoid duplicate effort.
cards.ok: Nest the Recruiting OU under the shared OU; move accounts between OUs
cards.bad: Remove accounts from the org and re-invite them
cards.why: SCPs inherit down nested OUs; moving accounts is cheap.

cards.scenario: Only the management account may buy Reserved Instances, for all current and future member accounts.
cards.ok: Deny SCP attached at the root
cards.bad: Deny SCP on a new OU holding the current accounts
cards.why: Root covers every present and future member; SCPs never affect the management account.

cards.scenario: Mobile app with custom authentication must get IAM role credentials.
cards.ok: OIDC provider plus Cognito identity pool (or SAML IdP in IAM)
cards.bad: API Gateway Lambda authorizer issuing JWTs
cards.why: Authorizers only authorize API calls; they never issue AWS credentials.

cards.scenario: Track cost per project and per environment; teams may use only pre-approved services.
cards.ok: Cost allocation tags plus Service Catalog portfolios
cards.bad: Custom budgets per project
cards.why: Budgets alert on thresholds; they don't attribute cost. Tags do.

cards.scenario: Stop brute-force SSH, log commands per session, keep port forwarding.
cards.ok: Session Manager; close port 22; log to S3/CloudWatch
cards.bad: Client VPN in front of SSH
cards.why: SSH stays open behind the VPN and session commands aren't logged.

cards.scenario: Encrypt traffic over Direct Connect using an IPsec VPN.
cards.ok: Create a public VIF for the VPN
cards.bad: Create a private VIF for the VPN
cards.why: The VPN endpoints are public IPs, so use a public VIF.

cards.scenario: One Direct Connect link must reach many VPCs and Regions.
cards.ok: Direct Connect Gateway with a VGW per VPC
cards.bad: One shared VGW attached to all the VPCs
cards.why: One VGW per VPC; allowed prefixes must cover the VPC CIDRs.

cards.scenario: Remote workstations must reach several peered VPCs.
cards.ok: Client VPN with one endpoint in the main VPC
cards.bad: A new transit gateway attached to every VPC
cards.why: One endpoint reaches peered VPCs; no new TGW needed.

cards.scenario: Expose a UDP service; non-UDP traffic must be blocked.
cards.ok: NLB with a NACL denying non-UDP
cards.bad: ALB with WAF rules
cards.why: WAF and ALB are layer 7; UDP needs NLB.

cards.scenario: Publish a service to other VPCs through PrivateLink.
cards.ok: Endpoint service backed by a Network Load Balancer
cards.bad: Endpoint service backed by an Application Load Balancer
cards.why: PrivateLink fronts NLB or GWLB, never ALB.

cards.scenario: Scale a fleet of security appliances transparently in the traffic path.
cards.ok: Gateway Load Balancer with an Auto Scaling group
cards.bad: NLB with static routes to each appliance
cards.why: GWLB is built for appliance fleets.

cards.scenario: Private-subnet instances need S3 without internet exposure.
cards.ok: S3 gateway endpoint
cards.bad: NAT gateway
cards.why: A gateway endpoint is private and free of NAT cost.

cards.scenario: Lock S3 access to one VPC only.
cards.ok: Endpoint policy plus bucket policy with aws:sourceVpce
cards.bad: Bucket policy allowing the VPC's private CIDR
cards.why: Private CIDRs are not visible to S3; the endpoint ID is.

cards.scenario: Inspect actual packet contents of traffic for analysis.
cards.ok: VPC Traffic Mirroring
cards.bad: VPC Flow Logs
cards.why: Flow Logs record metadata only, not payloads.

cards.scenario: Block one malicious IP address from reaching a subnet.
cards.ok: NACL deny rule
cards.bad: Security group deny rule
cards.why: Security groups can only allow; NACLs can deny.

cards.scenario: Associate a PHZ with a VPC in another account.
cards.ok: Create association authorization, then associate-vpc-with-hosted-zone
cards.bad: Delegate the zone with NS records
cards.why: Private zones use VPC association, not NS delegation.

cards.scenario: VPC must resolve on-prem or custom AD domain names.
cards.ok: Resolver outbound endpoint with a forwarding rule
cards.bad: Resolver inbound endpoint
cards.why: Outbound = queries leaving the VPC; inbound = into the VPC.

cards.scenario: Fast traffic shift needed, but clients cache DNS answers.
cards.ok: Global Accelerator traffic dials and weights
cards.bad: Lower Route 53 record weights
cards.why: DNS caching delays Route 53 changes; GA shifts at the edge.

cards.scenario: Static anycast IPs and acceleration for global S3 content.
cards.ok: CloudFront in front of S3
cards.bad: Global Accelerator with S3 as the endpoint
cards.why: Global Accelerator can't front S3.

cards.scenario: CloudFront returns 504 when the primary origin is down.
cards.ok: Origin group with failover origin
cards.bad: Create a second distribution with weighted DNS
cards.why: Origin groups handle origin failure inside CloudFront.

cards.scenario: Add S3 static content to a CloudFront distribution with an ALB origin.
cards.ok: New S3 origin with OAC and a path-pattern behavior
cards.bad: ALB listener rule forwarding to S3
cards.why: Behaviors route by path; an ALB can't proxy to S3.

cards.scenario: Simple header, URL or query-string rewrite at the edge.
cards.ok: CloudFront Functions
cards.bad: Lambda@Edge
cards.why: Use the lightest tool; Lambda@Edge is for network calls or body access.

cards.scenario: Static IP addresses needed in front of an ALB.
cards.ok: Put an NLB with static IPs in front of the ALB
cards.bad: Attach an Elastic IP to the ALB
cards.why: ALBs can't take EIPs; the NLB can.

cards.scenario: Multi-Region API Gateway must reroute automatically on full AND partial failures, using many metrics.
cards.ok: Route 53 ARC routing controls driven by alarms
cards.bad: Route 53 Evaluate Target Health
cards.why: Evaluate Target Health sees the endpoint only, not partial failures inside services.

cards.scenario: A/B test two site versions in two S3 buckets behind CloudFront; users must not notice.
cards.ok: Lambda@Edge origin request choosing the origin
cards.bad: Path-based behaviors with redirects
cards.why: Different paths and redirects are visible to users.

cards.scenario: Firewall Manager + Network Firewall strict order: allow SSH from trusted CIDRs, deny everything else.
cards.ok: Allow rule at the lowest priority number, deny-all after
cards.bad: Allow rule given the highest order number
cards.why: Rules evaluate from the lowest number; deny-all first blocks trusted SSH too.

cards.scenario: Interface endpoints in private subnets; connections fail. Which configuration change?
cards.ok: Allow 443 from the VPC on the endpoint ENI security group
cards.bad: Add a route table entry for the endpoint
cards.why: Interface endpoints are ENIs reached via DNS; routes are for gateway endpoints.

cards.scenario: NLB with instance-id targets, all healthy; customers can't connect from the office.
cards.ok: EC2 security group allows the office CIDR
cards.bad: EC2 security group allows the NLB subnets
cards.why: Instance-id targets preserve the client IP.

cards.scenario: Existing 10 Gbps DX with one private VIF needs redundancy; also reach a VPC in a second Region.
cards.ok: Second DX to the same Region plus a Direct Connect gateway
cards.bad: New DX connection to the second Region
cards.why: That adds a path to another VPC, not redundancy; the DX gateway is global.

cards.scenario: Regional REST API hit by botnets; only a few known companies call it twice daily; minimum cost.
cards.ok: WAF IP allow-list on the API plus usage plan and API key
cards.bad: CloudFront plus a WAF per-day rate rule
cards.why: WAF rate rules use short windows; CloudFront adds cost.

cards.scenario: Serverless upload app; users in many Regions need low-latency uploads to S3.
cards.ok: Edge-optimized API Gateway plus S3 Transfer Acceleration
cards.bad: Global Accelerator in front of CloudFront
cards.why: GA fronts ALB/NLB/EC2/EIP only, never CloudFront or S3.

cards.scenario: Several data centers on private fiber need HA, high-bandwidth, multi-Region AWS connectivity.
cards.ok: Direct Connect at each DC from different providers
cards.bad: Direct Connect with a VPN backup
cards.why: VPN backup is low bandwidth; diverse DX gives HA plus bandwidth.

cards.scenario: Copy 140 TB monthly on-prem to S3 over an existing 10 Gbps DX with a private VIF; LEAST expensive.
cards.ok: Add a public VIF on the same DX
cards.bad: S3 gateway endpoint over the private VIF
cards.why: Gateway endpoints aren't reachable from on-prem; a public VIF reaches S3.

cards.scenario: Import key material generated in the company's own HSM.
cards.ok: KMS key with Origin=EXTERNAL
cards.bad: KMS key created with automatic rotation
cards.why: External origin is how KMS accepts imported key material.

cards.scenario: Key must never leave the HSM, with high availability.
cards.ok: CloudHSM cluster spanning at least two AZs
cards.bad: Single-AZ CloudHSM instance
cards.why: Two AZs give HA; single node is a failure point.

cards.scenario: Reject unencrypted (HTTP) requests to an S3 bucket.
cards.ok: Bucket policy denying when aws:SecureTransport is false
cards.bad: Default SSE-KMS encryption on the bucket
cards.why: Encryption at rest doesn't force TLS in transit.

cards.scenario: Prevent objects from ever becoming public.
cards.ok: S3 Block Public Access
cards.bad: GuardDuty S3 protection
cards.why: GuardDuty only detects; Block Public Access prevents.

cards.scenario: Protect against layer 3/4 DDoS attacks with expert response.
cards.ok: Shield Advanced
cards.bad: WAF rate-based rule
cards.why: Network-layer DDoS is Shield; WAF is layer 7.

cards.scenario: Block SQL injection and XSS requests to an ALB.
cards.ok: AWS WAF
cards.bad: Shield Advanced
cards.why: SQLi/XSS are layer 7 application attacks, handled by WAF.

cards.scenario: Alarm when usage nears a service quota.
cards.ok: Alarm on AWS/Usage with SERVICE_QUOTA() math, plus SNS
cards.bad: Alarm on AWS/Usage using the SampleCount statistic
cards.why: Metric math against the quota gives the percentage of the limit.

cards.scenario: Discover PII stored in S3 buckets.
cards.ok: Amazon Macie
cards.bad: Amazon Inspector
cards.why: Macie finds sensitive data; Inspector scans for vulnerabilities.

cards.scenario: Audit who read which S3 objects.
cards.ok: CloudTrail data events
cards.bad: AWS Config
cards.why: Object reads are data-plane API calls, logged as data events.

cards.scenario: Scan Lambda functions for package CVEs and code flaws, skipping some.
cards.ok: Inspector standard and code scan; tag InspectorCodeExclusion
cards.bad: Exclude functions with an IAM policy
cards.why: Exclusion is done by tag, not IAM.

cards.scenario: Millions of unencrypted objects; many apps use the bucket; LEAST development effort to encrypt.
cards.ok: Default encryption plus S3 Inventory and Batch Operations copy-in-place
cards.bad: Copy objects to a new encrypted bucket
cards.why: A new bucket forces every app to change its bucket name.

cards.scenario: Keys need FIPS 140-2 Level 3, available business hours only, HA, MOST cost-effective.
cards.ok: CloudHSM multi-AZ cluster; delete and restore from backup off-hours
cards.bad: KMS with scheduled key disable/enable
cards.why: Exam treats KMS as Level 2 (real KMS gained Level 3 in 2023).

cards.scenario: Existing bucket with default settings; objects must not be deleted or overwritten for 5 years.
cards.ok: New bucket with Object Lock compliance mode; move the objects
cards.bad: Enable Object Lock on the existing bucket
cards.why: Exam key assumes Object Lock only on new buckets (real AWS allows existing since 2023).

cards.scenario: S3 behind CloudFront must enforce encryption in transit and at rest.
cards.ok: Bucket policy denying unencrypted PutObject plus CloudFront HTTPS redirect
cards.bad: aws:SecureTransport condition in S3 ACLs
cards.why: ACLs can't hold condition keys; only bucket policies can.

cards.scenario: PII bucket on SSE-S3; the security team must manage the keys for current and future objects.
cards.ok: SSE-KMS with a customer managed key; re-copy existing objects
cards.bad: SSE-S3 with a customer managed key
cards.why: SSE-S3 keys are always AWS-owned; that option is impossible.

cards.scenario: ECS behind ALB suffers attacks causing outages; prevent them, MOST cost-effective.
cards.ok: CloudFront with WAF, ALB locked by a custom header
cards.bad: Auto scaling plus caching
cards.why: Scaling and caching treat symptoms; WAF plus origin lock stops attacks.

cards.scenario: Serverless global app needs low latency and baseline DDoS protection.
cards.ok: CloudFront in front (Shield Standard included)
cards.bad: WAF web ACL for DDoS
cards.why: WAF filters L7 rules; baseline DDoS comes free with CloudFront.

cards.scenario: After a DDoS on EC2 + RDS serving static images, revamp security.
cards.ok: Route 53, CloudFront with static content on S3, WAF on CloudFront
cards.bad: WAF in front of the Auto Scaling group
cards.why: WAF attaches to CloudFront, ALB, API Gateway, AppSync, Cognito; never EC2/ASG.

cards.scenario: Detect an S3 object made public-read, alarm and auto-remediate.
cards.ok: CloudTrail data events plus EventBridge rule, then SNS and Lambda
cards.bad: S3 event notifications
cards.why: Event notifications can't filter by ACL, only event type and key prefix/suffix.

cards.scenario: Check service quotas every 15 minutes and alert at 80% utilization.
cards.ok: CloudWatch alarm on AWS/Usage with SERVICE_QUOTA() to SNS
cards.bad: AWS Budgets alert
cards.why: Budgets tracks cost and usage spend, never quotas.

cards.scenario: Lambda in a VPC must reach S3 or the internet. Where do you place it?
cards.ok: Private subnets with a gateway endpoint or NAT
cards.bad: A public subnet so the function gets a public IP
cards.why: Lambda ENIs never get public IPs.

cards.scenario: Containers must also run on other clouds. Which orchestrator?
cards.ok: Amazon EKS
cards.bad: Amazon ECS
cards.why: ECS is AWS-only; EKS is portable Kubernetes.

cards.scenario: Event-driven job runs longer than 15 minutes. Least overhead?
cards.ok: Fargate task started via EventBridge or Lambda RunTask
cards.bad: Lambda with maximum timeout and SQS retries
cards.why: Lambda maximum is 15 minutes.

cards.scenario: Expose one Lambda function over HTTPS, simplest possible.
cards.ok: Lambda Function URL
cards.bad: Fargate service behind an ALB
cards.why: Function URL is a built-in HTTPS endpoint; the rest is overbuilt.

cards.scenario: Many Lambda invocations exhaust RDS connections.
cards.ok: RDS Proxy, with the DB connection created outside the handler
cards.bad: A larger RDS instance with higher max_connections
cards.why: The proxy pools and reuses connections across invocations.

cards.scenario: Faster database failover while keeping application connections.
cards.ok: RDS Proxy in front of Aurora with replicas
cards.bad: RDS Multi-AZ with a short DNS TTL
cards.why: The proxy holds connections through failover.

cards.scenario: Stop one noisy Lambda function from starving the others.
cards.ok: Set reserved concurrency on that function
cards.bad: Enable provisioned concurrency on that function
cards.why: Reserved concurrency caps and guarantees; provisioned only pre-warms.

cards.scenario: Cut repeated backend calls for identical API requests.
cards.ok: Enable API Gateway caching
cards.bad: Raise Lambda memory for the backend
cards.why: A cache answers repeats without invoking the backend.

cards.scenario: API Gateway callers are IAM principals; secure and trace the API.
cards.ok: AWS_IAM (SigV4) authorization plus X-Ray
cards.bad: Enable CORS on the API
cards.why: CORS is a browser rule, not authentication.

cards.scenario: Different API clients need different request quotas.
cards.ok: Usage plans with API keys
cards.bad: Lambda reserved concurrency per client
cards.why: Usage plans throttle and meter per API key.

cards.scenario: Batch processing, least operational overhead.
cards.ok: AWS Batch on Spot with S3 for input and output
cards.bad: SQS plus a Spot ASG running your own scheduler
cards.why: Batch manages queues, retries and Spot for you.

cards.scenario: Tightly coupled HPC needing lowest inter-node latency.
cards.ok: Cluster placement group, EFA and FSx for Lustre
cards.bad: Spread placement group with EFS shared scratch
cards.why: Tight coupling needs cluster PG and EFA; EFS is too slow.

cards.scenario: Many small, lightly used apps, each on its own instance. Cut cost.
cards.ok: Containerize and bin-pack the tasks on ECS
cards.bad: Keep one instance per app and buy RIs
cards.why: Bin-packing removes idle instances.

cards.scenario: Deployment must keep full serving capacity throughout.
cards.ok: Beanstalk immutable or blue/green deployment
cards.bad: Beanstalk rolling deployment in batches
cards.why: Rolling takes instances out of service; immutable keeps full capacity.

cards.scenario: Gradual canary or linear traffic shift for a Lambda function.
cards.ok: SAM with CodeDeploy
cards.bad: Route 53 weighted records on the function
cards.why: CodeDeploy shifts Lambda alias traffic natively.

cards.scenario: Always-on production tier purchasing option.
cards.ok: On-Demand or Reserved Instances
cards.bad: Spot Instances for the lowest price
cards.why: Spot can be reclaimed at any time.

cards.scenario: Slow boot because of large static data. Fix it.
cards.ok: Bake the AMI and mount the data from EFS
cards.bad: Download the data in user data at launch
cards.why: Downloading at launch is exactly what makes boot slow.

cards.scenario: Cheapest resilient web tier.
cards.ok: Spot Fleet with On-Demand baseline across AZs behind an ALB
cards.bad: An all-Spot Auto Scaling group behind an ALB
cards.why: All Spot can vanish at once; keep a baseline.

cards.scenario: Dynamic web app plus queue-driven background jobs, cost-aware.
cards.ok: Fargate for web, Spot workers for the queue jobs
cards.bad: Spot for the web tier, On-Demand for workers
cards.why: Interruptible work belongs on Spot; user-facing web does not.

cards.scenario: Move an existing instance into a placement group.
cards.ok: Stop, modify the placement group, then start
cards.bad: Modify the placement group while it runs
cards.why: The instance must be stopped to change placement.

cards.scenario: CloudFormation template must always use the latest AMI.
cards.ok: SSM parameter type, then update the stack
cards.bad: Hardcode AMI IDs in a Mappings section
cards.why: The SSM parameter resolves the current AMI on update.

cards.scenario: Roll a new AMI to an ASG with no downtime via CloudFormation.
cards.ok: UpdatePolicy rolling update
cards.bad: A change set
cards.why: A change set only previews changes.

cards.scenario: CI/CD pipeline that deploys CloudFormation stacks.
cards.ok: CodePipeline with change set and CodeBuild
cards.bad: CodePipeline with CodeDeploy
cards.why: CodeDeploy deploys to compute, not stacks.

cards.scenario: Push real-time updates to many connected clients.
cards.ok: AWS AppSync subscriptions (WebSockets)
cards.bad: Clients polling an API every second
cards.why: Subscriptions push over WebSockets; polling wastes calls.

cards.scenario: Licensed software is bound to a MAC address.
cards.ok: Pre-licensed ENI pool with config in Parameter Store
cards.bad: Bake the license into the AMI
cards.why: The MAC belongs to the ENI, not the AMI.

cards.scenario: Debug an instance in an Auto Scaling group without it being replaced.
cards.ok: Suspend the Terminate process
cards.bad: Suspend the Launch process
cards.why: Terminate suspension stops the ASG killing the instance.

cards.scenario: Save instance data before the ASG terminates it.
cards.ok: Lifecycle hook on termination
cards.bad: Increase the deregistration delay
cards.why: The hook pauses termination so you can copy data.

cards.scenario: Steady EC2 usage in one family and Region, maximum savings.
cards.ok: EC2 Instance Savings Plan (up to 72%)
cards.bad: Compute Savings Plan (up to 66%)
cards.why: The EC2 Instance plan gives the deeper discount for steady EC2.

cards.scenario: Spend mixes EC2, Fargate and Lambda. Best commitment?
cards.ok: Compute Savings Plan
cards.bad: EC2 Instance Savings Plan
cards.why: Only the Compute plan spans EC2, Fargate and Lambda.

cards.scenario: Discount for steady RDS, ElastiCache or MemoryDB usage.
cards.ok: Reserved nodes
cards.bad: Compute Savings Plan
cards.why: Compute Savings Plans never cover databases or caches.

cards.scenario: Unexpected sales peaks with no time pattern; two EC2 behind an ALB respond slowly.
cards.ok: Target tracking on ALBRequestCountPerTarget
cards.bad: Scheduled scaling
cards.why: Scheduled actions only fit predictable peaks.

cards.scenario: DynamoDB auto scaling at 70% target; a predictable spike up to 300% causes throttling.
cards.ok: Scheduled scaling action ahead of the spike
cards.bad: Rely on target tracking or step scaling
cards.why: Reactive scaling lags a sudden spike; capacity must be ready first.

cards.scenario: Tightly coupled HPC; increase network throughput, reduce latency. Select three.
cards.ok: EFA instances, cluster placement in one AZ, hyperthreading disabled
cards.bad: Paravirtual (PV) AMI
cards.why: PV is legacy and slower; use HVM AMIs.

cards.scenario: Grid computing: timeouts between instances; adding instances didn't help; LEAST effort.
cards.ok: Relaunch into a cluster placement group
cards.bad: Enable ENA
cards.why: Instances already use ENA; the issue is inter-node latency.

cards.scenario: Runbook describes install and config; LEAST overhead; allow future changes.
cards.ok: CloudFormation plus user data for install and config
cards.bad: CloudFormation for infra, manual runbook for software
cards.why: Automate the whole runbook; change via stack updates.

cards.scenario: AWS Batch with a custom AMI, restartable jobs; reduce overhead and cost.
cards.ok: Managed EC2 compute environment with Spot
cards.bad: Fargate Spot
cards.why: Fargate can't use a custom AMI.

cards.scenario: SQS standard workers aren't scaling with load; MOST scalable approach.
cards.ok: Target tracking on backlog per instance
cards.bad: Scale on ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible
cards.why: Queue depth doesn't change in proportion to fleet size.

cards.scenario: PHP LAMP developer, little AWS expertise, stable traffic, predictable monthly pricing.
cards.ok: Amazon Lightsail
cards.bad: Elastic Beanstalk with DynamoDB
cards.why: Pay-per-resource pricing and a new NoSQL DB break the asks.

cards.scenario: EKS with highly variable stateless pods launched quickly; optimize node resilience.
cards.ok: Topology spread constraints across AZs
cards.bad: Under-provisioned Cluster Autoscaler
cards.why: Resilience means surviving an AZ failure, not capacity sizing.

cards.scenario: Remote users find a latency-sensitive desktop client slow; minimize changes and costs.
cards.ok: Stream the app with AppStream 2.0
cards.bad: Add ElastiCache and RDS Multi-AZ
cards.why: Caching the DB doesn't fix a slow remote desktop client.

cards.scenario: 350 remote staff need full Windows and Linux desktops with on-prem AD and MFA.
cards.ok: WorkSpaces with AD Connector and RADIUS MFA
cards.bad: AppStream 2.0
cards.why: AppStream streams apps, not full desktops.

cards.scenario: Expense app with Friday bursts; HA; LEAST operational overhead.
cards.ok: S3 + CloudFront front end, API Gateway + Lambda back end
cards.bad: ECS behind an ALB
cards.why: Containers still need cluster capacity management unless Fargate.

cards.scenario: gp2 3 TB volume needs +3,000 IOPS per instance; MOST cost-efficient.
cards.ok: Grow the gp2 volume by 1 TB (or move to gp3)
cards.bad: Move the data to EFS
cards.why: gp2 = 3 IOPS per GiB; EFS adds cost and no IOPS guarantee.

cards.scenario: Serverless API returns 504 on image loads; DynamoDB fine; find the root cause.
cards.ok: X-Ray traces plus Lambda CloudWatch Logs
cards.bad: API Gateway execution logging
cards.why: Gateway logs confirm the 504, not where the time goes.

cards.scenario: RDS MySQL reads are slow and replicas have no shared endpoint. Quick, cheap fix?
cards.ok: Add ElastiCache in front of the database
cards.bad: Migrate the database to another engine
cards.why: Caching is the quick fix; do not migrate.

cards.scenario: Read-heavy RDS workload on a budget.
cards.ok: Read replicas plus ElastiCache and sharding
cards.bad: A bigger instance with Provisioned IOPS
cards.why: Scale reads out, not up.

cards.scenario: Aurora must absorb write bursts.
cards.ok: Buffer the writes with SQS
cards.bad: Aurora Auto Scaling to add more writers
cards.why: Aurora Auto Scaling adds readers only.

cards.scenario: Multi-Region relational DB with one writer and RPO under one second.
cards.ok: Aurora Global Database
cards.bad: Cross-Region copy of nightly Aurora snapshots
cards.why: Global Database replicates continuously with RPO under 1 s.

cards.scenario: Active-active multi-Region NoSQL writes.
cards.ok: DynamoDB global tables
cards.bad: Aurora Global Database
cards.why: Aurora Global has a single writer Region.

cards.scenario: Oracle RAC is required.
cards.ok: Self-manage Oracle on EC2
cards.bad: Amazon RDS for Oracle
cards.why: RDS has no RAC support.

cards.scenario: The same stream record must reach many separate applications.
cards.ok: Kinesis Data Streams
cards.bad: Amazon SQS
cards.why: SQS delivers each message to one consumer, then deletes it.

cards.scenario: Multiple KDS consumers lag behind each other.
cards.ok: Enhanced Fan-Out
cards.bad: Lengthen the stream retention period
cards.why: Each fan-out consumer gets its own dedicated throughput.

cards.scenario: Transform streaming records, then land them in S3.
cards.ok: Kinesis Data Firehose with Lambda
cards.bad: KDS plus a custom EC2 consumer writing to S3
cards.why: Firehose transforms and delivers with no servers.

cards.scenario: Classic exam answer: deliver a KDS stream into Redshift.
cards.ok: Kinesis Data Firehose
cards.bad: A custom EC2 consumer running COPY
cards.why: Firehose is the managed delivery path to Redshift.

cards.scenario: Ad hoc or nightly SQL over ORC/Parquet in S3.
cards.ok: Athena with Glue Data Catalog
cards.bad: A Redshift cluster
cards.why: Serverless Athena queries S3 in place; no cluster to run.

cards.scenario: Analyze WAF logs cheaply with SQL.
cards.ok: Firehose to S3, then Athena
cards.bad: CloudWatch Logs exported into RDS
cards.why: Athena queries S3 logs serverlessly.

cards.scenario: Redshift read bursts from many concurrent queries.
cards.ok: Concurrency scaling
cards.bad: Offload the queries to EMR or RDS
cards.why: Concurrency scaling adds read capacity on demand.

cards.scenario: Step Functions must process messages from an SQS queue.
cards.ok: A Lambda poller starts the state machine
cards.bad: SQS queue as direct Step Functions input
cards.why: Step Functions cannot take SQS as direct input.

cards.scenario: DynamoDB time-series data with cheap expiry of old data.
cards.ok: Table per period; device ID key, timestamp sort key
cards.bad: One table, deleting old items with scans
cards.why: Dropping a whole old table is cheap and fast.

cards.scenario: DynamoDB with steady, predictable throughput.
cards.ok: Reserved capacity
cards.bad: On-demand capacity mode
cards.why: Steady load is cheaper with reserved capacity.

cards.scenario: Redshift disaster recovery in another Region.
cards.ok: Automated snapshots with cross-Region snapshot copy
cards.bad: A second cluster reloaded nightly with COPY
cards.why: Snapshot copy is the built-in DR path.

cards.scenario: Cross-Region snapshot copy of a KMS-encrypted Redshift cluster.
cards.ok: Create a snapshot copy grant first
cards.bad: Share the source Region KMS key directly
cards.why: The destination Region needs a grant for its KMS key.

cards.scenario: One-off EMR job, minimize cost.
cards.ok: On-Demand master and core nodes, Spot task nodes
cards.bad: Reserved Instances for all nodes
cards.why: A one-off job should not commit to RIs.

cards.scenario: OpenSearch with aging data, cost-optimized.
cards.ok: Hot, UltraWarm and cold tiers
cards.bad: Keep all data on larger hot nodes
cards.why: Tiering moves older data to cheaper storage.

cards.scenario: Aurora global DB: low-latency local reads and writes with read-after-write; test DR.
cards.ok: Write forwarding on the secondary; managed failover for tests
cards.bad: Read from the secondary, write to the primary
cards.why: Secondary reads may be stale, breaking read-after-write.

cards.scenario: DynamoDB on-demand with bursts and a few hot keys; reduce cost, LEAST overhead.
cards.ok: DAX plus provisioned capacity with auto scaling
cards.bad: DAX plus Savings Plans
cards.why: Savings Plans never cover DynamoDB.

cards.scenario: DynamoDB dev table provisioned for peak; write-heavy weekend peak; optimize cost.
cards.ok: On-demand capacity
cards.bad: On-demand capacity plus DAX
cards.why: DAX caches reads only; it never helps writes.

cards.scenario: 15 GB/day of statistics in S3 queried by Athena with date ranges; optimal performance.
cards.ok: Parquet/ORC with date partitions
cards.bad: A separate bucket per date range
cards.why: Partitions prune scanned data for date queries.

cards.scenario: Copy KMS-encrypted Redshift snapshots to another Region for DR.
cards.ok: Snapshot copy grant for a destination-Region key; enable copy in source
cards.bad: Copy grant in the source Region with the source key
cards.why: KMS keys are Regional; the grant must be in the destination.

cards.scenario: Fully serverless sensor ingestion into DynamoDB; no manual capacity planning.
cards.ok: SQS plus Lambda writing to DynamoDB
cards.bad: Firehose writing directly to DynamoDB
cards.why: DynamoDB isn't a Firehose destination.

cards.scenario: Gaming leaderboard: in-memory, single-digit ms, highly available.
cards.ok: ElastiCache Redis sorted sets (or DynamoDB with DAX)
cards.bad: DynamoDB alone
cards.why: DynamoDB is disk-based; the stem says in-memory.

cards.scenario: Retire tape archives and also analyze the content of stored media.
cards.ok: File Gateway plus Rekognition
cards.bad: Tape Gateway
cards.why: Tape Gateway stores virtual tapes; you cannot process them in place.

cards.scenario: Windows SMB file shares in AWS, migrate the data.
cards.ok: FSx for Windows File Server with DataSync
cards.bad: Amazon EFS
cards.why: EFS is Linux (NFS) only.

cards.scenario: Interactive NGINX and MySQL application needs hosting.
cards.ok: EC2 or containers with a database
cards.bad: S3 static website hosting
cards.why: S3 website hosting serves static files only.

cards.scenario: S3 static website shows nothing after setup.
cards.ok: Make the bucket objects publicly readable
cards.bad: Wait for DNS propagation
cards.why: The missing piece is public read access.

cards.scenario: On-premises iSCSI volumes: hot subset local, full data in AWS.
cards.ok: Volume Gateway cached volumes
cards.bad: Volume Gateway stored volumes
cards.why: Stored keeps a full local copy; cached keeps only hot data.

cards.scenario: S3 replication needs a time-bound SLA.
cards.ok: S3 Replication Time Control
cards.bad: Standard cross-Region replication
cards.why: RTC carries a replication-time SLA.

cards.scenario: Users far from the bucket upload large files slowly.
cards.ok: S3 Transfer Acceleration
cards.bad: Add a bucket in the user's Region only
cards.why: Acceleration uses edge locations over the AWS backbone.

cards.scenario: Bulk transfer would take over a week on the link.
cards.ok: Snowball Edge, then land in S3 and use lifecycle
cards.bad: Keep copying over the link
cards.why: 1 Gbps moves roughly 10.8 TB/day; slower than shipping.

cards.scenario: Import an existing VM as-is into AWS.
cards.ok: VM Import
cards.bad: AWS Application Migration Service (MGN)
cards.why: VM Import converts an image as-is; MGN is for continuous replication.

cards.scenario: Continuous block-level replication for server cutover.
cards.ok: AWS Application Migration Service (MGN)
cards.bad: VM Import
cards.why: VM Import is a one-time image conversion.

cards.scenario: Build the TCO case for migrating to AWS.
cards.ok: Migration Evaluator
cards.bad: Application Discovery Service
cards.why: Migration Evaluator produces the business case.

cards.scenario: Discover on-premises servers and dependencies before migrating.
cards.ok: Application Discovery Service
cards.bad: Migration Evaluator
cards.why: Discovery collects server inventory and dependency data.

cards.scenario: Migrate a heterogeneous database with minimal downtime.
cards.ok: SCT for schema, DMS with CDC
cards.bad: DMS alone with no schema conversion
cards.why: Different engines need schema conversion plus ongoing change capture.

cards.scenario: Move an app to a managed platform with no code rewrite.
cards.ok: Replatform
cards.bad: Refactor into microservices
cards.why: Replatform swaps the platform; refactor rewrites code.

cards.scenario: Managed SFTP into S3 with a fixed IP and security groups.
cards.ok: Transfer Family with a VPC endpoint
cards.bad: SFTP server on EC2 with custom scripts
cards.why: VPC endpoint allows an Elastic IP and security groups.

cards.scenario: One shared dataset copied onto many EBS volumes is slow.
cards.ok: One EFS file system with Provisioned Throughput
cards.bad: EFS in Max I/O mode
cards.why: Max I/O adds latency; it does not guarantee throughput.

cards.scenario: Replicate RDS MySQL to an on-premises replica.
cards.ok: VPN, mysqldump and external replication
cards.bad: Create an RDS read replica on premises
cards.why: RDS read replicas cannot be placed on premises.

cards.scenario: App must survive RDS Multi-AZ failover.
cards.ok: Connect by DNS endpoint; the CNAME flips to the standby
cards.bad: Hardcode the primary instance IP
cards.why: Failover changes the CNAME target, not the IP.

cards.scenario: Infrastructure as code for repeatable stacks.
cards.ok: CloudFormation
cards.bad: Elastic Beanstalk
cards.why: Beanstalk deploys apps; CloudFormation defines infrastructure.

cards.scenario: Push notifications to a mobile app.
cards.ok: SNS Mobile Push
cards.bad: SNS SMS
cards.why: App push uses platform endpoints, not text messages.

cards.scenario: DR with an RTO of hours, lowest cost.
cards.ok: Backup and restore
cards.bad: Multi-site active-active
cards.why: Hours of downtime allows the cheapest tier.

cards.scenario: DR with an RTO of tens of minutes.
cards.ok: Pilot light
cards.bad: Backup and restore
cards.why: Core is pre-provisioned; backup/restore is too slow.

cards.scenario: DR with an RTO of minutes.
cards.ok: Warm standby
cards.bad: Pilot light
cards.why: Warm standby runs a scaled-down full copy.

cards.scenario: DR with near-zero RTO.
cards.ok: Multi-site active-active
cards.bad: Warm standby
cards.why: Only active-active is near zero.

cards.scenario: Meet a Regional disaster recovery requirement.
cards.ok: Cross-Region DR strategy
cards.bad: RDS Multi-AZ
cards.why: Multi-AZ is high availability, not DR.

cards.scenario: Convert video on demand for adaptive streaming.
cards.ok: MediaConvert with HLS output
cards.bad: Transcribe
cards.why: Transcribe converts speech to text, not video.

cards.scenario: Devices publish telemetry over MQTT.
cards.ok: AWS IoT Core
cards.bad: Kinesis Data Streams
cards.why: IoT Core is the managed MQTT broker.

cards.scenario: ML inference at an offline edge site.
cards.ok: AWS IoT Greengrass
cards.bad: Lambda in a Region
cards.why: Greengrass runs locally without connectivity.

cards.scenario: Orchestrate a long, stateful multi-step workflow.
cards.ok: AWS Step Functions
cards.bad: A chain of SQS queues
cards.why: Step Functions tracks state, retries and branching.

cards.scenario: Intelligent-Tiering; rarely accessed after 180 days; must retrieve within 6 hours; cheapest.
cards.ok: Archive Access tier
cards.bad: Deep Archive Access tier
cards.why: Deep Archive can take up to 12 hours; Archive Access restores within ~5 hours.

cards.scenario: Static files on-prem shared by several servers over NFS; migrate to S3, keep one copy.
cards.ok: S3 File Gateway
cards.bad: Volume Gateway
cards.why: Volume Gateway is iSCSI block storage, not S3 objects shared via NFS.

cards.scenario: Move an on-prem VMware app to EC2, preserving software and configuration.
cards.ok: Export OVF to S3, then VM Import
cards.bad: DataSync to an FSx for Windows datastore
cards.why: A VM isn't a file share; VM Import keeps it as-is.

cards.scenario: Move 25 TB to S3 fast: 1 Gbps internet, 500 Mbps Direct Connect.
cards.ok: S3 Transfer Acceleration over the 1 Gbps link
cards.bad: Snowball
cards.why: ~2-3 days online beats shipping; Snowball pays off past ~1 week.
